title: Lesson 5: Overview of the Bible
description: Welcome to a guided tour of the most important book you will ever read. The Bible isn't a single book. It is a library of 66 unique volumes written by 40 authors across 1,500 years. Learning how this life-changing book is organized will help you understand it and remember how the story of God fits together.

blocks.text: In the last lesson, you saw that deep roots grow down into Jesus, the Good Soil. One of the deepest roots in the Christian life is the Word of God. In the next three lessons you are going to learn how to receive that Word with more confidence: this lesson gives you the map, the next lesson takes you on the road trip, and the final lesson hands you the tools to dig into any passage on your own.

blocks.alt: A bookshelf displaying all 66 books of the Bible organized by section

blocks.title: A Library, Not a Single Book
blocks.text:
Because the Bible is a library and not a single book, its contents are incredibly diverse. There are kings, shepherds, fishermen, doctors, tax collectors, and prophets among the writers. They wrote in different countries, in different centuries, in different circumstances. And yet the whole library tells one unified story from beginning to end, as we will learn in the next lesson.

That is remarkable. No human editor could have planned this across fifteen centuries. This unity is one of the strongest evidences that God Himself was behind every page. As Paul wrote to Timothy:

"All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work." (2 Timothy 3:16-17)

"Breathed out by God." That means when you open the Bible, you are not reading someone's personal journal or philosophical opinion. You are reading words that the living God intended for you to have. And because He organized this library with purpose, understanding how it is structured will help you read it with much greater confidence.

A common question is, if Scripture was written long ago and copied for centuries, can it still be trusted? Christians do not believe the Bible is reliable because the copying process was casual. God preserved His Word through real history, through public reading, careful copying, and many manuscripts that allow scholars to compare copies and identify small copying differences.

The Dead Sea Scrolls are one helpful example. They include biblical manuscripts copied before the time of Jesus, including a nearly complete copy of Isaiah, and they showed that the Old Testament text had been preserved with remarkable care over many centuries. That does not mean every manuscript copy is letter-for-letter identical; most differences are spelling, word order, or small copying variations. It does mean the message of Scripture has not been lost. You are not building your life on a rumor that changed in the shadows. You are opening a Word God has carried faithfully through time.

Old Testament & New Testament

The Bible is divided into two major parts: the Old Testament and the New Testament. The word "testament" means covenant, a binding promise between God and His people. The Old Testament tells the story of God creating the world, choosing a people (Israel), giving them His law, and promising that a Savior would come. The New Testament tells the story of that Savior arriving in Jesus, the birth of the church, and the future hope of all things being made new.

The Old Testament has 39 books. The New Testament has 27. Together they form the complete Word of God. Some people struggle with the Old Testament because it feels distant or confusing. But here is the key: the Old Testament is not a different story with a different God. It is the first part of the same story, and every page of it points forward to Jesus. You cannot fully understand the New Testament without the Old, and you cannot fully understand the Old without the New.

Here is one more reason to trust the Old Testament: Jesus did. He quoted it constantly, argued from it, and treated every word of it as completely authoritative. If the eternal Son of God read those pages and accepted them without reservation, that is all the endorsement they need.

The Bible Is "Your Very Life"

The Bible is organized like those books on that bookshelf, but was never meant to stay on a shelf. One of the most famous passages in all of Scripture comes from the very first section you explored, the Law. Moses spoke these words to Israel just before they crossed into the Promised Land:

Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise.

This is the Shema, and Jesus called it the greatest commandment. Since you began this Growing Deep course, you have already seen these words in Lesson 1, where you learned that loving God is not a burden but a response to a Father who loved you first. Now you know exactly where that passage lives - Deuteronomy, the Law section, the first shelf on your bookshelf. That is what knowing the map does. It connects what you have already learned to where it lives in Scripture.

Notice what Moses says to do with God's Word: put it on your heart, teach it to your children, talk about it when you sit down and when you get up, when you are home and when you are on the road. This is not a book to study once and set aside. It is meant to become part of how you think, how you talk, and how you live - and when you do, God promises that it will go well with you.
It is no empty word for you, but your very life, and by this word you shall live long in the land that you are going over the Jordan to possess.

No empty word. Your very life. Jesus echoed this same truth when Satan tempted Him in the wilderness. You can find it in Matthew 4, right on the Gospels shelf: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. The life that food gives you keeps you going for a few more hours. The life that God's Word gives you is firm, abundant, and never runs out.

A Word on Translations

The Bible was originally written in Hebrew (most of the Old Testament), Aramaic (small portions), and Greek (the New Testament). Because most readers do not read those languages, English translations matter. There are many good ones, and choosing a translation can feel confusing. Here is a simple way to think about it.

Some translations lean toward word-for-word accuracy, staying as close to the original language as possible. The ESV (English Standard Version) and NASB are examples of this. Others lean toward thought-for-thought clarity, translating the meaning of each sentence in a way that feels more natural to a modern reader. The NIV and NLT are examples of this. Many faithful translations lean in one direction or the other. A more word-for-word translation is helpful for careful study. A more thought-for-thought translation is helpful for steady reading, especially when a passage feels difficult.

This course uses the ESV, which gives you a reliable, readable translation that stays very close to the original words. Whatever translation you use, the most important thing is that you are reading the Bible consistently. The best translation is the one you will actually open.
Lesson 5 Review

You now have the map. The Bible is a library of 66 books arranged in clear sections: Law, History, Poetry, Prophets, Gospels, Acts, Letters, and Revelation. The Old Testament tells the story of God creating, choosing, and promising. The New Testament tells the story of God fulfilling every promise in Jesus. In the next lesson you will take the road trip through the one big story that ties all of these books together.
